newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Bangui truce extended for 10 days.
newsitem.headline: Bangui truce extended for 10 days.

text.p: A truce between dissident soldiers and African peacekeepers in the Central African Republic capital was consolidated and extended for 10 days on Wednesday, to help defuse a crisis that killed around 100 people, mediators said.

The extended truce, which became a formal ceasefire from 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Wednesday, would enable mediators to put back on track a derailed January 25 peace deal that ended three army mutinies in under a year, they added.

"During the 10 days the mutineers should return to barracks and continue handing in their weapons to the French embassy," the ceasefire deal said. "Negotiations should continue to ensure a lasting agreement."
The head of the peacekeeping force General Edouard Edjo Nkili and Captain Anicet Saulet, leader of the mutineers, signed the ceasefire.

Mali's respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure, architect of the January deal, and former colonial power France's ambassador Jean-Marc Simon will be guarantors of the dissident soldiers' security.
A week of clashes between former army mutineers and peacekeepers followed a June 20 incident involving the two sides. The Red Cross says about 100 people, mostly civilians, died in the fighting.
Relief workers say up to 60,000 people fled their homes for the relative safety of the countryside. More fled on Wednesday before the deal to extend a four-day truce agreed on Saturday.
The dissidents, a minority of whom had not returned to their units under the January peace deal, agreed to hand over their heavy weapons to France's ambassador in Bangui under the four-day truce.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 began as pay protests but evolved into a bid to topple President Ange-Felix Patasse, a civilian from the north, elected in 1993. A third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.

French troops intervened to halt that fighting and then handed over to the peacekeepers under the January deal. The dissident soldiers criticise the presence of Chadians among the peacekeepers. They say Patasse hired Chadians as a militia.
Most of the mutineers were from the minority Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
